# How to Turn Your Saved Articles and Notes into a Personal Podcast with NotebookLM

> **In short:** Google's NotebookLM can read up to about 50 of your own sources — links, PDFs, Google Docs, pasted text — and turn them into a roughly 10-to-20-minute audio conversation between two AI voices. It is free with a Google account, and the audio stays grounded in your sources rather than the open internet.

You've got a folder full of articles, a few PDFs you keep meaning to read, and a commute that could use better company. NotebookLM is a free Google tool built for exactly this kind of "I'll get to it later" pile. Point it at your reading list, ask for an audio overview, and two synthetic hosts will chat through the highlights while you walk, drive, or wash dishes.

## Before you start
- **A Google account** — any personal Gmail address works.
- **A web browser** on a phone, tablet, or computer — NotebookLM runs in the browser, no install needed.
- **3 to 5 sources** to feed it: web links, PDFs on your computer, Google Docs from your Drive, YouTube links, or text you can copy and paste.
- **About 15 to 20 minutes total** for setup plus the first audio generation (the audio itself usually takes a few minutes to cook).
- One honest note: the audio is a *summary* of your sources, not a verbatim read-aloud. If you need every word spoken, this is not the right tool.

## Step 1 — Open NotebookLM and create a fresh notebook
In your browser, go to the NotebookLM homepage and sign in with your Google account when prompted. Once you're in, look for a button that says something like **New Notebook** (it may say *Create* or show a plus-sign **+**). Click it. You'll see a clean workspace with a left sidebar, a center area that invites you to add a source, and a small notes section. If your screen looks different — Google updates its products often — look for a clearly empty page with wording like **Add your first source** in the middle.

💬 Example: type a short name like "Weekend reading" or "Q3 research" into the notebook title field so you can find it later.

You'll know it worked when a new notebook opens with an empty source list and the Studio panel on the right is ready.

## Step 2 — Drop in your first article or PDF
Look for a button or panel labeled **Add source** (it might say *Upload* or *Insert*). Click it and you'll see a small window offering several options: paste a website link, upload a file from your computer, pick a Google Drive document, paste raw text, or add a YouTube link. Pick whichever matches what you saved. For a typical "I've been meaning to read this" article, copy the URL from your browser and paste it in. A short loading indicator appears while NotebookLM reads the page, then the source shows up in the left-hand Sources list with a small icon and the page title.

💬 Example: paste the URL of one long article you've been putting off.

You'll know it worked when the source appears in the list with its title — usually within a few seconds for a normal web page, longer for big PDFs.

## Step 3 — Build out your reading list
Repeat the same **Add source** action for each article, PDF, or document you want covered. Aim for **3 to 10 sources** in one notebook — enough variety for a meaty conversation, not so many that the summary loses focus. Each source gets its own row in the Sources list. You can mix types freely: two web articles, one PDF report, one Google Doc of meeting notes, and one YouTube link all work together.

💬 Example: add 4 items — a long-form article, a PDF report you downloaded last week, a Google Doc with your own notes, and one more link.

You'll know it worked when every source shows up in the Sources panel and none of them show a red error icon. If one fails to load, remove it and try again — usually a sign-in or link problem.

## Step 4 — Generate the Audio Overview
Now look at the **Studio** panel on the right side of the screen. Inside it, look for an option labeled something like **Audio Overview**. Click the button that says **Generate** (the exact wording can change as Google updates the product). A small status message appears — usually "Generating audio overview…" — and NotebookLM begins writing a script between two AI hosts, then voicing it. This usually takes **2 to 5 minutes**, depending on how much material you fed it. You can leave the tab open and do something else; it'll be ready when you come back.

💬 Example: type an optional instruction in the custom prompt box if you see one, such as "Focus on the parts about pricing strategy."

You'll know it worked when a small audio player appears in the Studio panel with a play button and a total length (typically between 8 and 25 minutes).

## Step 5 — Listen, save, or try again
Press the **play button** ▶ on the audio player. Two voices start chatting through your sources — one asks questions, the other explains, they bounce ideas back and forth like a real conversation. You can pause, drag the slider, and adjust playback speed. Look for a small download or share button near the player if you want to save the file for offline listening; if you don't see one, the audio stays inside NotebookLM for that session. If the summary misses the point or sounds off, click **Regenerate** (or a similar refresh icon) — each generation is a fresh script, and quality varies.

💬 Example: while listening, jot down a question in the Notes section on the right so you can ask NotebookLM's chat about it after.

You'll know it worked when the two hosts are clearly discussing the *content* of your sources — naming the same people, companies, or ideas from your PDFs and links — instead of generic filler.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting 30 sources at once.** The summary gets thinner and more generic the more you add. Stick to a tight theme: 3 to 10 sources that actually belong together.
- **Trying to feed paywalled or login-only pages.** NotebookLM can only read what's publicly accessible on the open web. For paywalled articles, download the PDF or paste the text manually.
- **Expecting the audio to quote your sources verbatim.** It summarizes and discusses them — it does not read them aloud. If you need a literal read-aloud, this tool won't deliver.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Got a stack of "read later" articles about a topic you care about — gardening, parenting, fitness — feed them in and listen on a walk. It's a friendlier way to catch up than scrolling.
- **For your business or work:** Drop in your project briefs, meeting notes, and a few industry reports. The audio overview becomes a quick briefing you can listen to on the way to a meeting.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one notebook, one topic, and three sources you've already saved. That's all you need to hear whether the format clicks for you.

## Try it now
Open NotebookLM in your browser, create a new notebook, and paste in the link to one article you've been meaning to read. Hit the Audio Overview generate button. By the time you make a cup of coffee, you'll have your first mini-podcast.
